text: [Mathlib’s quadratic radical](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/QuadraticForm/Radical.lean#L35) requires both q(k)=0 and b(k,x)=0 for every x. Thus a subgroup contained there is contained in the polar radical by retaining the second condition. Viewing an additive subgroup as a ℤ-submodule does not enlarge it. The converse is not asserted: polar vanishing alone need not force q(k)=0. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Quadratic.lean#L772) passes.
The polar quotient built using this inclusion evaluates to the original pairing.

This is A/K with q([x])=q(x) in ℚ/ℤ. The hypothesis says every k∈K has q(k)=0 and b(k,x)=0 for all x, so q(x+k)=q(x). [Mathlib’s quotient lift](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/QuadraticForm/Radical.lean#L81) therefore makes the value representative-independent; the stored polar pairing is the corresponding bilinear quotient. No nondegeneracy is assumed. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Quadratic.lean#L764) passes, Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Quadratic.lean#L772) passes.
The descended quadratic value agrees with q on representatives.
The descended polar pairing agrees with b on both representatives.

The map sends x to its class in A/K and is additive, exactly the canonical map of [Mathlib’s quotient](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/Defs.lean#L61). The radical hypothesis ensures that the target also carries the descended quadratic form; it does not change the underlying group quotient. Its kernel is K, so this map is generally not injective. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Quadratic.lean#L758) passes, Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Quadratic.lean#L804) passes.
The map is the canonical quotient class on every input.
The zero class has precisely K as its preimage.

The descended quadratic form evaluates on [x] to q(x). In [Mathlib’s quotient lift](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/QuadraticForm/Radical.lean#L81), K lies in the quadratic radical, meaning both q(K)=0 and b(K,A)=0; hence changing x by k∈K changes the value by q(k)+b(x,k)=0. This explains representative independence without assuming the polar pairing is nondegenerate. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Quadratic.lean#L955) passes.
The orthogonal-quotient specialization uses this representative formula.

Every element of A/K is a class [x], so the canonical additive map onto this quadratic quotient is surjective, as for [Mathlib’s quotient](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/Defs.lean#L61). The quadratic-radical assumption is required to equip that group quotient with q; surjectivity itself is purely about its carrier. It asserts existence of representatives, not a distinguished representative. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Quadratic.lean#L794) passes.
The elimination theorem explicitly obtains a representative using this surjectivity.

An element has zero quotient class exactly when it belongs to K. This is the kernel criterion for [Mathlib’s quotient](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/Defs.lean#L61); the ℤ-submodule attached to K has exactly the same elements. The required quadratic-radical inclusion makes q descend, but does not enlarge the subgroup killed by the quotient map. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Quadratic.lean#L814) passes.
The zero criterion yields the exact difference-in-K criterion for equality of representatives.

This subgroup consists of the elements of H that also lie in H⊥, viewed inside H⊥. It is generally H∩H⊥, not all of H: no isotropy is assumed here. When q vanishes on H, polarization gives H≤H⊥ and this becomes the copy of H used in [Nikulin §1.4](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im1677)’s orthogonal quotient. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Quadratic.lean#L857) passes.
Membership is exactly membership of the underlying element in H.

The input x already belongs to H⊥ by its type. Membership in the subgroup H∩H⊥ inside H⊥ therefore asks only whether its underlying element belongs to H. This records the precise intersection needed for [Nikulin §1.4](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im1677)’s orthogonal quotient, without silently assuming that an arbitrary H is isotropic. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Quadratic.lean#L865) passes.
Restricting a supplied q-isotropy hypothesis uses this exact membership translation.

The restricted quadratic form has the same value q(x) on each x∈H⊥. If q vanishes on H, it consequently vanishes on the subgroup H∩H⊥ inside H⊥. This is restriction of the supplied quadratic-isotropy hypothesis in [Nikulin §1.4](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im1677)’s sense; vanishing of the polar pairing alone is never substituted for it. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Quadratic.lean#L874) passes.
The restricted q-vanishing condition combines with polar-radical containment to permit descent.

For h∈H and x∈H⊥, symmetry gives b(h,x)=0; the hypothesis separately gives q(h)=0. Together these put H’s copy inside [Mathlib’s quadratic radical](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/QuadraticForm/Radical.lean#L35) of the restricted form. Consequently q(x+h)=q(x), which is precisely the representative-independence condition needed to form the quadratic quotient of H⊥ by H. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Quadratic.lean#L955) passes.
The quotient enabled by this inclusion has the claimed representative value.

The construction restricts q to H⊥ and quotients by H, as in [Nikulin §1.4](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im1677). Its explicit hypothesis q|H=0 gives H≤H⊥; for x∈H⊥ and h∈H, q(x+h)=q(x)+q(h)+b(x,h)=q(x). Thus q descends independently of representatives. The resulting polar pairing may still be degenerate unless additional hypotheses are supplied. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Quadratic.lean#L955) passes, Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Quadratic.lean#L966) passes.
The quotient quadratic value is the original q on representatives.
The quotient polar pairing is the original b on representatives.

Forgetting q after forming H⊥/H gives the same finite bilinear module as restricting and quotienting b first. Both constructions use the identical group quotient and pairing on representatives, consistent with [Nikulin §1.4](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im1677)’s induced form. The hypothesis is quadratic isotropy; it ensures that this comparison really uses H, rather than only H∩H⊥. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Quadratic.lean#L1035) passes.
The comparison transfers the exact polar-radical criterion for nondegeneracy.

The domain is H⊥, and the map sends x to [x] in H⊥/H, the canonical projection of [Mathlib’s quotient](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/Defs.lean#L61). Quadratic isotropy ensures H≤H⊥ and permits q to descend; it does not supply a projection from all of A onto this quotient. The displayed additive-map type correctly preserves that domain restriction. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Quadratic.lean#L921) passes, Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Quadratic.lean#L995) passes.
Every input is sent to its canonical quotient class.
An input has zero class precisely when its underlying element belongs to H.

For x∈H⊥, the induced quadratic value of [x] is q(x), matching [Nikulin §1.4](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im1677)’s orthogonal reduction. Both restrictions matter: q(h)=0 for h∈H and b(x,h)=0 imply q(x+h)=q(x). The representative is an element of H⊥ by its type, so the equation does not claim a quotient formula for arbitrary elements of A. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Orthogonal/GaussSum.lean#L58) passes.
The native isotropic-reduction identity consumes the descended form and actual representative multiplicities.

Each element of the orthogonal quotient has a representative in H⊥. This is surjectivity of [Mathlib’s quotient](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/Defs.lean#L61) applied to the restricted group, not a claim that every element of A lies in H⊥. Quadratic isotropy is present to define the descended quadratic form; no choice of a canonical representative or nondegeneracy is needed. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Quadratic.lean#L986) passes.
The quotient elimination theorem obtains a representative using this surjectivity.

For x already in H⊥, its class vanishes exactly when x∈H. The literal subgroup divided out is H∩H⊥ inside H⊥, so the input’s type removes the extra membership condition. This is [Mathlib’s quotient](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/Defs.lean#L61)’s zero-class criterion with the correct restricted carrier; quadratic isotropy justifies writing the quotient as H⊥/H. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Quadratic.lean#L1005) passes.
Equality of two classes becomes the exact condition that their difference lies in H.

Nondegeneracy here means the polar pairing is perfect. For q-isotropic H, the radical of b restricted to H⊥ is H+rad(b); after quotienting by H it vanishes exactly when rad(b)≤H. This matches the orthogonal reduction of [Nikulin §1.4](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im1677), with a precise extension to degenerate ambient forms. The radical is bilinear, not merely q’s zero set. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Quadratic.lean#L1042) passes.
The nondegenerate ambient case specializes the radical-containment criterion.

With a perfect polar pairing, |H⊥|·|H|=|A|. Quadratic isotropy supplies H≤H⊥, so quotienting divides |H⊥| by |H| and yields |H⊥/H|·|H|²=|A|, as in [Nikulin §1.4](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im1677)’s finite orthogonal reduction. Nat.card is ordinary finite cardinality here; the displayed multiplicative identity involves no rounded natural-number division. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Orthogonal/GaussSum.lean#L82) passes.
The native normalization argument uses this exact cardinality identity to compare Gauss sums.

The explicit hypothesis makes the ambient polar radical zero. It is therefore contained in H, and the orthogonal quotient’s polar radical vanishes by the preceding criterion. This is the nondegenerate reduction of [Nikulin §1.4](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im1677), with q-isotropy ensuring the quadratic form descends. It does not assert that arbitrary restrictions of nondegenerate forms remain nondegenerate. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Orthogonal/GaussSum.lean#L82) passes.
The native Gauss-sign comparison explicitly consumes nondegeneracy of this quotient.

This finite group is A/K with pairing b([x],[y])=b(x,y). Since K pairs to zero with every element, changing either representative leaves the value unchanged; symmetry handles both arguments in [Mathlib’s bilinear lift](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/Bilinear.lean#L28). The construction allows degenerate pairings and imposes no quadratic-form condition, because only the bilinear pairing is being descended. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/RadicalQuotient.lean#L126) passes, Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/RadicalQuotient.lean#L148) passes.
The descended pairing evaluates on arbitrary representatives as b.
The group quotient kills exactly K.

An enumeration lists the roots after mapping coefficients into the integral domain L, retaining every multiplicity, as in [Milne, §2, p.31](https://jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/FT.pdf#page=31). Multiset equality expresses exactly this. For the zero polynomial, Mathlib stores an empty root multiset: an empty enumeration therefore does not assert that its set of zeros is empty. Controls: [card_roots](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/RootEnumeration.lean#L103) passes; [injective_iff_separable_map](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/RootEnumeration.lean#L249) passes.
The number of entries of an enumeration is the number of roots of `f` in `L`.

**An enumeration is injective exactly when the polynomial is separable.** If `y` enumerates
the roots in the field `E` of a polynomial `f` whose image in `E` is nonzero, and has at least as
many entries as the degree of that image, then `y` is injective if and only if the image of `f` in
`E` is separable.

This equivalence unfolds the definition: each index contributes one entry, so repeated values count repeatedly, matching [Milne, §2, p.31](https://jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/FT.pdf#page=31). Equality of these multisets is stronger than equality of sets. The target algebra is an integral domain; the coefficient map need not be injective, and the zero polynomial uses Mathlib’s empty root multiset. Controls: [isRootEnumeration_comp_equiv_iff](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/RootEnumeration.lean#L94) passes; [splits](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/RootEnumeration.lean#L126) passes.
Reindexing an enumeration along a bijection gives an enumeration.

**An enumeration forces splitting.** If `x` enumerates the roots of `f` in `L` and has at
least as many entries as the degree of the image of `f` in `L` (for instance, at least
`f.natDegree` entries), then `f` splits in `L`.

A bijection from degree-many indices to the distinct root set already lists every root with multiplicity one: distinct-root count saturates the multiplicity bound ([Milne, Proposition 1.7](https://jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/FT.pdf#page=10)). No extra separability assumption is needed. If the mapped polynomial is zero, its stored root set is empty, so the assumed bijection forces the original natural degree to be zero. Controls: [natDegree_map](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/RootEnumeration.lean#L149) passes; [map_eq_C_mul_prod_X_sub_C](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/RootEnumeration.lean#L161) passes.

A degree-sized root enumeration makes base change preserve the degree. This includes
annihilating base change in degree zero.

A degree-sized root enumeration factors the mapped polynomial with the image of its source
leading coefficient, including zero and annihilating base change in degree zero.

A root list with as many entries as the original natural degree gives the mapped polynomial as its mapped leading coefficient times all numbered linear factors. Repetitions retain multiplicity ([Milne, §2, p.31](https://jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/FT.pdf#page=31)). Injectivity of the coefficient map is unnecessary: a constant killed by it yields zero times the empty product, correctly equal to zero. Controls: [leadingCoeff_map](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/RootEnumeration.lean#L156) passes; [eq_C_mul_prod_X_sub_C](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/RootEnumeration.lean#L134) passes.
A degree-sized root enumeration makes base change preserve the leading coefficient.

An enumeration with at least as many entries as the degree of the mapped polynomial gives
its complete linear factorization, including the leading coefficient.

An enumeration with at least the mapped degree in entries supplies all linear factors, repeated with multiplicity, together with the mapped polynomial’s leading coefficient. This is [Milne, §2, p.31](https://jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/FT.pdf#page=31)’s factorization, valid here over an integral domain. The degree inequality ensures completeness; for zero the leading coefficient vanishes and the empty product is one. Controls: [splits](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/RootEnumeration.lean#L126) passes; [map_eq_C_mul_prod_X_sub_C](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/RootEnumeration.lean#L161) passes.

**An enumeration forces splitting.** If `x` enumerates the roots of `f` in `L` and has at
least as many entries as the degree of the image of `f` in `L` (for instance, at least
`f.natDegree` entries), then `f` splits in `L`.

A degree-sized root enumeration factors the mapped polynomial with the image of its source
leading coefficient, including zero and annihilating base change in degree zero.

Degree-many enumerated roots prevent the mapped polynomial’s natural degree from dropping, so its highest coefficient is the image of the original highest coefficient. The root bound is the familiar one in [Milne, Proposition 1.7](https://jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/FT.pdf#page=10). No injective coefficient map is assumed: a constant may map to zero, whose leading coefficient is zero. Controls: [natDegree_map](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/RootEnumeration.lean#L149) passes; [map_eq_C_mul_prod_X_sub_C](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/RootEnumeration.lean#L161) passes.

A degree-sized root enumeration makes base change preserve the degree. This includes
annihilating base change in degree zero.

A degree-sized root enumeration factors the mapped polynomial with the image of its source
leading coefficient, including zero and annihilating base change in degree zero.

An enumeration with exactly the original natural degree in entries forces equality of the original and mapped natural degrees: root count bounds the latter below, while coefficient mapping bounds it above ([Milne, Proposition 1.7](https://jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/FT.pdf#page=10)). The zero polynomial has natural degree zero, so annihilating a constant is compatible with the conclusion; coefficient-map injectivity is unnecessary. Controls: [leadingCoeff_map](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/RootEnumeration.lean#L156) passes; [map_eq_C_mul_prod_X_sub_C](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/RootEnumeration.lean#L161) passes.
A degree-sized root enumeration makes base change preserve the leading coefficient.

A degree-sized root enumeration factors the mapped polynomial with the image of its source
leading coefficient, including zero and annihilating base change in degree zero.

The entries count roots with multiplicity in the integral domain L. Their number cannot exceed the mapped polynomial’s natural degree, by the root bound underlying [Milne, Proposition 1.7](https://jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/FT.pdf#page=10); the stated reverse inequality therefore forces equality. This is about the mapped degree, allowing noninjective coefficient maps. Zero contributes zero stored roots and natural degree zero. Controls: [splits](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/RootEnumeration.lean#L126) passes; [eq_C_mul_prod_X_sub_C](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/RootEnumeration.lean#L134) passes.

**An enumeration forces splitting.** If `x` enumerates the roots of `f` in `L` and has at
least as many entries as the degree of the image of `f` in `L` (for instance, at least
`f.natDegree` entries), then `f` splits in `L`.

An enumeration with at least as many entries as the degree of the mapped polynomial gives
its complete linear factorization, including the leading coefficient.

If the list has at least the mapped natural degree in entries, the root bound forces equality, hence a complete linear factorization with multiplicities ([Milne, §2, p.31](https://jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/FT.pdf#page=31)). The integral-domain hypothesis supports this criterion. Mathlib includes zero among split polynomials, consistent with its empty root multiset and natural degree zero; no separability is asserted. Controls: [eq_C_mul_prod_X_sub_C](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/RootEnumeration.lean#L134) passes; [injective_iff_separable_map](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/RootEnumeration.lean#L249) passes.

An enumeration with at least as many entries as the degree of the mapped polynomial gives
its complete linear factorization, including the leading coefficient.

**An enumeration is injective exactly when the polynomial is separable.** If `y` enumerates
the roots in the field `E` of a polynomial `f` whose image in `E` is nonzero, and has at least as
many entries as the degree of that image, then `y` is injective if and only if the image of `f` in
`E` is separable.

Counting the defining multiset equality gives one root occurrence per index, including repeated values as in [Milne, §2, p.31](https://jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/FT.pdf#page=31). Thus the conclusion counts roots with multiplicity, not distinct roots, and requires no splitting assumption. A polynomial may have fewer roots here than its degree; for zero the stored multiset and any enumeration are empty. Controls: [card_le_natDegree](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/RootEnumeration.lean#L108) passes; [range_eq_rootSet](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/RootEnumeration.lean#L112) passes.
An enumeration has at most `f.natDegree` entries.
The entries of an enumeration are exactly the roots of `f` in `L`.

When the finite index set has the mapped natural degree in elements, splitting is equivalent to listing all roots with multiplicity, as in [Milne, §2, p.31](https://jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/FT.pdf#page=31). Reindexing the root multiset supplies the list, without choosing a canonical ordering or assuming separability. Constants, including zero, have natural degree zero and use the empty list. Controls: [splits](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/RootEnumeration.lean#L126) passes; [isRootEnumeration_comp_equiv_iff](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/RootEnumeration.lean#L94) passes.

**An enumeration forces splitting.** If `x` enumerates the roots of `f` in `L` and has at
least as many entries as the degree of the image of `f` in `L` (for instance, at least
`f.natDegree` entries), then `f` splits in `L`.
Reindexing an enumeration along a bijection gives an enumeration.

For nonnegative inputs, this is the greatest natural number no larger than the input; negative inputs return zero. On the reals this clips ordinary floor at zero. Partial orders are also permitted: the floor axioms leave inputs incomparable with zero unspecified. Compared with [Aspnes §4.7](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Floor/Defs.lean#L125).

This returns the least natural number at least as large as the input. On the reals it is ordinary ceiling clipped at zero, so every nonpositive input gives zero. The defining equivalence is ceiling(a)≤n exactly when a≤n; it remains meaningful under the permitted partial order. Compared with [Aspnes §4.7](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Floor/Defs.lean#L129).

This is the greatest integer no larger than the input, with the usual downward rounding on the reals. Negative values are retained: floor(−1/2)=−1. The supplied floor structure guarantees existence and the comparison rule for every integer; the definition does not assume that every ordered ring automatically has such a structure. Compared with [Aspnes §4.7](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Floor/Defs.lean#L256).

This is the least integer no smaller than the input, agreeing with ordinary upward rounding on the reals. It can be negative: ceiling(−3/2)=−1. Its comparison rule characterizes the answer uniquely. Existence is part of the supplied floor structure, rather than an unstated property of every linearly ordered ring. Compared with [Aspnes §4.7](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Floor/Defs.lean#L260).

The natural-valued floor, cast back into the original number system, is at most its input when that input is nonnegative. The hypothesis is necessary because negative real inputs have natural floor zero. The proof uses precisely the defining comparison rule, without imposing completeness or compatibility of multiplication with order. Compared with [Aspnes §4.7](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Floor/Semiring.lean#L47).

Increasing an input cannot decrease its natural-valued floor. This includes negative inputs, whose floors are zero, and inputs on opposite sides of zero. Equality is allowed: the function is monotone, not strictly increasing. The linear order allows the proof to separate the nonpositive and nonnegative cases. Compared with [Aspnes §4.7](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Floor/Semiring.lean#L93).

The natural-valued floor is zero exactly when the input is less than one. This includes all negative inputs because this floor is clipped at zero. The threshold is strict: at one the answer is one. For the ordinary integer-valued floor, the corresponding zero interval would instead be [0,1). Compared with [Aspnes §4.7](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Floor/Semiring.lean#L127).

Casting a natural number into the ambient number system and then taking its natural-valued floor recovers that number exactly, including zero. This is the familiar fact that floor fixes whole numbers. The floor assumptions themselves ensure that natural-number casts preserve and reflect order; no separate characteristic-zero hypothesis is missing. Compared with [Aspnes §4.7](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Floor/Semiring.lean#L66).

The natural-valued floor is positive exactly when the input is at least one. Merely being positive is insufficient: a real input between zero and one still rounds down to zero. The statement includes the endpoint one and handles negative inputs automatically through the natural floor’s zero-clipping convention. Compared with [Aspnes §4.7](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Floor/Semiring.lean#L110).

Taking natural floor after subtracting one agrees with subtracting one from the natural floor. The subtraction on the right stops at zero: for inputs below one, both sides are zero. The left uses the ambient subtraction, whose compatibility with order is explicitly assumed; no assumption that the input exceeds one is needed. Compared with [Aspnes §4.7](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Floor/Semiring.lean#L329).

The natural ceiling of a is at most n exactly when a is at most the natural number n after casting. This is the least-upper-natural characterization of ceiling. It holds even for negative inputs and n=0, and the hypotheses require only a partial order together with the supplied floor structure. Compared with [Aspnes §4.7](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Floor/Defs.lean#L156).

For a nonnegative input, its natural-valued ceiling is strictly less than the input plus one. Thus rounding upward adds less than one, including at whole numbers where it adds zero. The nonnegative hypothesis protects against the clipping convention: sufficiently negative real inputs have ceiling zero and would violate this inequality. Compared with [Aspnes §4.7](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Floor/Semiring.lean#L357).

An integer z is the floor of a exactly when z≤a<z+1, with the integer endpoints cast into the ambient ring. The lower endpoint is included and the upper endpoint excluded, so this characterizes a unique unit interval. Negative inputs and negative integers are fully covered; there is no clipping at zero. Compared with [Aspnes §4.7](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Floor/Ring.lean#L139).

Adding one to an input adds exactly one to its integer-valued floor. This is the usual translation rule, valid for negative inputs as well as positive ones; for example, crossing zero creates no exceptional case. The source explicitly assumes that addition preserves order, which makes translation of the floor inequalities legitimate. Compared with [Aspnes §4.7](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Floor/Ring.lean#L191).

Two numbers with the same integer-valued floor differ in absolute value by less than one, because both lie in the same half-open unit interval. The strict bound includes the lower endpoint. No nonnegativity assumption is needed, and the converse is not asserted: nearby numbers can lie across an integer boundary. Compared with [Aspnes §4.7](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Floor/Ring.lean#L243).

Casting n−m from the naturals preserves subtraction provided m≤n. That condition matters: natural subtraction stops at zero, whereas subtraction in the target additive group uses genuine inverses. For example, casting natural 1−2 gives zero, not −1. Equality m=n is allowed, and no characteristic-zero or multiplicative structure is required. Compared with [Judson §3.2](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Int/Cast/Basic.lean#L36).

For a positive natural number n, casting its predecessor gives the cast of n minus one. Positivity excludes the truncated-subtraction exception at zero: natural 0−1 is zero, while in the integers 0−1=−1. The target only needs an additive group with a designated one, not a field or an injective cast. Compared with [Judson §3.2](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Int/Cast/Basic.lean#L40).

When n divides m exactly and its cast is nonzero, casting the natural quotient m/n agrees with division after casting. Natural division normally discards the remainder, so exact divisibility is essential. The nonzero condition is imposed in the target, correctly excluding denominators that become zero in positive characteristic. Compared with [Judson §§2.2,16.2](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Nat/Cast/Field.lean#L31).

For natural numbers m,n with n>0, both quotients equal the floor of the ordinary rational quotient m/n. Casting from naturals to integers preserves this rounding: 5/2 gives two on both sides, without requiring divisibility. At n=0, Lean defines both quotients to be zero. Compared with [Aspnes §8.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Int/Init.lean#L207).

The cast of “a choose two” equals a(a−1)/2 in any division ring where two is nonzero. Subtraction and division on the right occur in that ring, not in the naturals. The identity includes a=0 and a=1, and allows positive characteristic other than two; characteristic zero is unnecessary. Compared with [Aspnes §11.2](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Nat/Choose/Cast.lean#L45).

For an embedding g:Y→Z, a map f:X→Y is continuous exactly when g∘f is continuous. The embedding identifies Y with its image carrying the inherited topology, so continuity into that subspace is tested in Z. This is Semmes’s subspace-continuity criterion; no surjectivity onto Z is required. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L246).

If f and g are continuous and their composite g∘f is an embedding, then f is an embedding. Injectivity follows from the composite. Every open set in X is pulled back from Z, hence from an open set in Y by continuity of g. Both continuity hypotheses are retained. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L219).

When f induces the topology of X from Y, a subset s is dense in X exactly when every point of f(X) lies in the closure of f(s). This follows from pulling back closure under the induced topology. The target closure need not be all of Y, and f need not be injective. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L171).

Suppose Y has exactly the topology pulled back from Z along g. Then g∘f induces the topology of X exactly when f does. Pulling back a topology in two steps gives the same open sets as pulling it back along the composite. Neither map is required to be injective. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L78).

When g induces Y’s topology from Z, a function converges to y exactly when its composite with g converges to g(y). This holds along any filter, including the one used for ordinary sequences. Neighborhoods of y are pulled back from neighborhoods of g(y), so neither first countability nor injectivity is needed. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L117).

For a quotient map f:X→Y, a map g:Y→Z is continuous exactly when g∘f is continuous. The topology on Y is defined by openness of preimages under the surjective map f, giving precisely Semmes’s universal property of the quotient topology. No open-map or closed-map assumption is added. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L358).

A map is a quotient map exactly when it is surjective and a target subset is closed precisely when its preimage is closed. This is Semmes’s closed-set formulation of the quotient topology, obtained by taking complements in the open-set definition. Surjectivity is explicitly retained, and no separation assumption appears. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L326).

A continuous surjective open map is a quotient map. Continuity makes preimages of open target sets open; conversely, an open preimage has open image, and surjectivity makes that image the original target set. This verifies Semmes’s quotient-topology definition. Openness alone does not include continuity, so it remains a separate hypothesis. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L434).

A continuous surjective closed map is a quotient map. A target set with closed preimage is the image of that preimage, hence closed; continuity supplies the converse. This matches Semmes’s closed-set criterion. Closed-map means preservation of closed images, and the theorem separately requires continuity and surjectivity. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L576).

A continuous injective open map identifies its domain homeomorphically with an open subspace of the target. Continuity gives one direction; openness makes the inverse on the image continuous. The image is open because the whole domain is open. This is the usual subspace and inverse-continuity interpretation of an open embedding. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L761).

A continuous injective closed map is a homeomorphism onto a closed subspace of its target. Closed images make its inverse on the image continuous, while the image of the whole domain is closed. This follows from the subspace closed-set and continuity criteria; no compactness or Hausdorffness assumption is required. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L847).

For a continuous open map f, the preimage of the closure of any target subset equals the closure of its preimage. Continuity gives one inclusion. For the reverse, each domain neighborhood has an image neighborhood that meets the target subset. This uses both hypotheses and requires neither injectivity nor surjectivity. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L454).

A continuous open map pulls back the boundary of any subset to the boundary of its preimage. Write the boundary as the intersection of the closures of the set and its complement; the closure identity applies to both, and preimages preserve intersections and complements. No separation or surjectivity assumption is needed. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L468).

For a continuous open map f, the preimage of a subset’s interior is the interior of its preimage. Continuity supplies open preimages in one direction; openness sends a domain neighborhood contained in the preimage to a target neighborhood inside the subset. Both hypotheses are explicit, with no surjectivity requirement. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L444).

Under a closed embedding, a domain subset is closed exactly when its image is closed in the whole target. The forward direction uses the closed range together with the inherited topology. The reverse follows by taking a continuous preimage and using injectivity. This strengthens mere relative closedness in the image. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L833).

A space embedded in a discrete space is itself discrete. Every domain subset is the preimage of its image, by injectivity; that image is open in the discrete target, and continuity makes its preimage open. This is the inherited-topology principle, and it also applies to the empty domain. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L260).

If f induces the domain topology from its target, a domain set is open exactly when it is the preimage of some open target set. This is the inverse-image version of Semmes’s relative-open-set definition. It does not require injectivity, and it does not assert that the image of every open set is open. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L157).

If g:Y→Z is a closed embedding, then g∘f is a closed embedding exactly when f:X→Y is. Embeddings compose and are reflected through an embedding; closedness of the composite image corresponds to closedness of f(X) because g preserves and reflects closed subsets. No surjectivity of either map is assumed. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L867).

The neighborhood-filter inequality means that images of neighborhoods of x are neighborhoods of f(x). Therefore every point in the image of an open set has a neighborhood inside that image, making the map open. Filter order uses reverse inclusion of families of sets; no continuity assumption is hidden here. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L417).

A bijection with continuous inverse is an open map: the image of each open domain set is its preimage under the inverse. This is exactly Semmes’s inverse-continuity criterion. The two inverse identities are both supplied; continuity of the forward map is not assumed, so no homeomorphism is asserted. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L429).
